history: Received 6 mg of pegylated granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF) one week prior

diagnostic_test.name: Flow cytometry
procedure: Peripheral blood sample analyzed by immunophenotyping
Cells stained for CD34 and CD117 markers

branch.interpretation: The patient's abnormal blood counts, including elevated white blood cell count with a left shift and presence of blasts, in the context of recent chemotherapy and G-CSF administration, suggest a reactive process rather than de novo acute leukemia.
branch.result: The dynamic changes in laboratory values along with clinical context favor observation with repeat labs rather than immediate invasive testing or therapy.

diagnostic_options.description: Perform a bone marrow biopsy to evaluate for acute leukemia.
evidence_for: Abnormal differential with presence of blasts
evidence_against: Recent pegylated G-CSF administration can induce reactive changes
Improvement in platelet count observed without specific leukemia treatment
Clinical context supports a reactive process rather than primary hematologic malignancy
diagnostic_options.final_verdict: Not recommended currently due to the likelihood of a reactive process.

diagnostic_options.description: Prescribe all-trans retinoic acid for suspected acute promyelocytic leukemia.
evidence_for: The presence of blasts might raise concern for leukemia
evidence_against: Lack of other clinical features of acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL)
No typical APL marker abnormalities mentioned

diagnostic_options.description: Repeat complete blood cell count with differential in 1 to 2 weeks to monitor trends.
evidence_for: Current laboratory abnormalities may be due to a reactive process from G-CSF
Some laboratory parameters are improving (e.g., increasing platelets)
Allows time to observe dynamic changes before proceeding with invasive testing
evidence_against: Requires careful monitoring to ensure no progression to an overt hematologic malignancy
diagnostic_options.final_verdict: Recommended as the next step in management.

diagnostic_options.description: Start cytoreductive therapy with hydroxyurea to reduce the white blood cell count.
evidence_for: Elevated white blood cell count might prompt consideration of cytoreduction
evidence_against: The elevation is likely reactive rather than due to a primary myeloproliferative disorder
No symptoms of hyperviscosity or complications warranting immediate cytoreduction

conclusion: The best next step is to repeat the complete blood cell count with differential in 1 to 2 weeks to monitor trends, supporting a reactive process related to recent G-CSF administration rather than acute leukemia.
